newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serb refugees arrive to vote.
newsitem.headline: Serb refugees arrive to vote.

text.p: Hundreds of Serb refugees arrived back in Bosnia on a dilapidated train early on Saturday to cast ballots in landmark elections later in the day.
Many said they had been pressured to make the trip by threats they could lose their precious status as refugees in neighbouring Serbia unless they returned to vote.
Around 60,000 Bosnian Serb refugees living in Serbia are expected to vote in the Bosnian Serb Republic and around 10,000 in the Moslem-Croat Federation.

Getting off the train from Belgrade at Bijeljina in northeast Bosnia, the refugees were directed by megaphone through knee-deep mud and darkness to reach buses provided by Bosnian Serb authorities to take them to polling centres.
More than 4,000 polling stations were expected open across Bosnia at 0500 GMT for the critical post-war election widely seen as the turning point in the country's fortunes.
Most of train travellers said they had not seen their homes in Bosnia since 1992, when war broke out.
Western observers said many of the refugees themselves had been forced by Serbian authorities to come to Bosnia to cast their ballots.

"I will lose all my rights as a refugee (in Serbia) unless I can show a mark on my refugee card that I have voted," a woman said. Despite the pressure, she said she would vote for the Bosnian Serb affiliate party of Serbia's ruling Socialists. Her words were echoed by many other voters, who have had months of exposure in Serbia to state television supporting the Socialist Party of the Bosnian Serb Republic, the main election opposition in Serb areas to the hardline ruling Serb Democratic Party (SDS).
The SDS was founded by indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic, the former protege of Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic.
Milosevic fell out with Karadzic over the hardliner's reluctance to accept international peace plans in 1993.
"This train is a symbol of all our tragedies. Milosevic set us on this path to destruction and now he wants us to bale him out," said one refugee voter, Milan, a medical worker.
"We have fought each other, we have destroyed our lives, we have ethnically cleansed each other and now in his mind we are supposed to forgive each other."
Milosevic wants the SDS to win the elections in Serb-controlled Bosnia but also wants a strong opposition there, according to Western diplomats in Belgrade.

Few refugees said they believed Bosnia's first post-war election would lead to the unified country envisaged in the Dayton peace treaty signed last December. Some said they knew nothing about the election campaigns or candidates.

"Nobody has explained to us who will be on the list. We have no idea who we will vote for because we have not seen the list (of names on the ballot)," said Mile Kiso earlier, as the train left Belgrade railway station.
